question: Who belongs to the exception?

positions.position: All people meeting the qualities.
positions.reasons: Ṭabarī, Jishumī and Qurṭubī make the exception general; al-Ālūsī calls named persons foremost examples.

positions.position: ʿAlī and Salmān are named among its believers.
positions.reasons: Ibn ʿAbbās names them; al-Ālūsī denies an exclusive limit.

positions.position: Abū Bakr, ʿUmar, ʿUthmān and ʿAlī represent the four successive qualities.
positions.reasons: Ubayy transmits a Prophetic gloss; Ibn ʿAbbās repeated it from the pulpit. Some reports name Abū Jahl as the person in loss.

positions.position: God's chosen people, with faith applied to ʿAlī's wilayah.
positions.reasons: Al-Qummī reports this from al-Ṣādiq; counsel teaches descendants and successors.

turns_on: Whether the names limit the exception or exemplify it.

question: Who is the person in loss from whom believers are excepted?

positions.position: The warning concerns humanity generally, including named opponents.
positions.reasons: Wāḥidī treats individual unbelievers as included under the general wording, since believers are excepted.

positions.position: Al-Walīd ibn al-Mughīra, al-ʿĀṣ ibn Wāʾil and al-Aswad ibn ʿAbd al-Muṭṭalib are named.
positions.reasons: ʿAṭāʾ transmits this from Ibn ʿAbbās.

positions.position: Abū Lahab is named.
positions.reasons: Wāḥidī transmits this from Muqātil.

positions.position: Abū Jahl is named.
positions.reasons: A report attributed to the Prophet names him; the four-Companion interpretation likewise uses him.

turns_on: Whether the generic warning is applied to one opponent or several.

question: What human subject does this exception address?

positions.position: A morally responsible human, individually and socially accountable.
positions.reasons: Bint al-Shāṭiʾ surveys Qurʾānic al-insān as tested, articulate and entrusted with duty; she accepts al-Rāghib's sociability derivation but stresses obligations beyond mere membership of humankind.

question: Why can singular al-insān take this plural exception?

positions.position: It denotes humanity collectively despite singular form.
positions.reasons: Majāz cites 70:19–22, 69:47 and al-Nābighah's poem; Ṭabarī, Qurṭubī and Burhān agree.

question: What loss remains for a believer lacking some qualities?
words: إِلَّا ٱلَّذِينَ ءَامَنُوا۟ وَعَمِلُوا۟ ٱلصَّٰلِحَٰتِ وَتَوَاصَوْا۟ بِٱلْحَقِّ وَتَوَاصَوْا۟ بِٱلصَّبْرِ

positions.position: Full exemption requires all four; omission entails some loss.
positions.reasons: Muḥammad b. Kaʿb says faith alone is insufficient; Rāzī and Elmalılı require both personal and communal duties. Elmalılı rejects the Murjiʾite denial of loss from inaction.

positions.position: Grave sinners outside the exception suffer eternal loss.
positions.reasons: Rāzī reports threat-focused interpreters; some Muʿtazilites draw the same conclusion from the restricted exception.

positions.position: Loss has degrees: an unbeliever's is eternal; a sinner may be punished or lose higher reward.
positions.reasons: Al-Ālūsī and Bursawī distinguish pardoned and unpardoned sinners; Ibn ʿĀshūr cites 11:114; Ṭabāṭabāʾī adds intercession. Al-Māturīdī's further replies seem strained to al-Ālūsī.

positions.position: Omitted extra counsel may lose extra reward without utter ruin.
positions.reasons: Al-Tibyān contrasts the stricter exception here with another; enjoining may be individual, communal or recommended.

turns_on: Whether khusr necessarily entails eternal punishment.

question: What does faith mean here?

positions.position: Assent to God, revelation, messengers and the Last Day.
positions.reasons: Ṭabarī adds duty to obey; Biqāʿī names angels and scriptures; Ṭabāṭabāʾī says denial of a messenger or Last Day contradicts faith.

positions.position: A living connection to God directing moral life.
positions.reasons: Quṭb describes liberation, equality, dignity, calm, responsibility and lasting reward, citing 40:19 and 83:26.

positions.position: Certain knowledge of God as sole agent, beyond time's veil.
positions.reasons: Qāshānī and Bursawī describe lasting virtue and inward light.

question: How are faith and deeds related?

positions.position: Deeds are outside faith's definition, or the coordination repeats faith.
positions.reasons: Rāzī's first group rejects analogy with 33:7 and 2:98; repetition is possible but not the default. Bint al-Shāṭiʾ also cites 3:81.

positions.position: Deeds express or overlap faith; mentioning them emphasizes action.
positions.reasons: Al-Ḥalīmī allows repetition because deeds include faith. Bint al-Shāṭiʾ calls it specification; Iṣlāḥī says faith is foundation. Quṭb cites 14:18 and 24:39 for fruitless works without faith.

turns_on: Whether coordination separates concepts or highlights a manifestation.

question: What are righteous deeds?

positions.position: All prescribed good, including duties, avoiding sin, and benefit to others.
positions.reasons: Ṭabarī and Ibn ʿĀshūr read the class comprehensively; Biqāʿī mentions worship and commerce; Ibn ʿĀshūr repentance; Elmalılı charity and juristic sources.

question: What makes deeds righteous?

positions.position: Their goodness lies in inherent benefit.
positions.reasons: Rāzī reports the Muʿtazilite inference.

positions.position: The wording leaves open inherent benefit versus divine command.
positions.reasons: Rāzī reports the Ashʿarite reply.

turns_on: Whether the adjective gives a ground independent of command.

question: What does tawāṣaw imply?

positions.position: Reciprocal, regular advice and support, practiced by those offering it.
positions.reasons: Thaʿlabī and Baghawī say urge; Qurṭubī adds love; Bint al-Shāṭiʾ traces binding and bequest. Ibn ʿĀshūr recalls 2:44 and 89:18; Biqāʿī emphasizes gentleness.

question: Why use past-tense tawāṣaw?

positions.position: It describes and praises a continuing practice coordinated with earlier verbs.
positions.reasons: Rāzī sees praise and persistence; Nasafī coordination; Biqāʿī encouragement to enter the faith.

question: What is the truth urged in mutual counsel?

positions.position: The Qurʾān or God's Book.
positions.reasons: Al-Ḥasan and Qatāda often give this gloss; Ṭabarī explains its commands and prohibitions.

positions.position: God Himself, the Real.
positions.reasons: Kaʿb and al-Suddī identify God; Damghānī lists twelve senses and cites 23:71; Tustarī and Sūlamī speak of the Real.

positions.position: Faith and divine unity.
positions.reasons: Muqātil and Yaḥyā b. Sallām focus on monotheism; Abū Isḥāq adds steadfast faith in the Messenger.

positions.position: Established, undeniable right embracing belief, worship, justice and religious good.
positions.reasons: Zamakhsharī, Bayḍāwī and Nasafī give the broad sense; Biqāʿī includes lawful speech and acts. Bint al-Shāṭiʾ traces firmness and rights; Iṣlāḥī includes certainty, rational truth and moral obligation, including poor people's rights.

positions.position: A dying person's charge to heirs to die as Muslims.
positions.reasons: Māwardī and Ṭabrisī transmit this; Study Quran compares 3:102.

turns_on: Whether ḥaqq selects a particular object or comprehensive right.

question: Why add counsel in truth after personal deeds?

positions.position: Believers must complete others by teaching, enjoining good and opposing wrong.
positions.reasons: Rāzī cites 66:6; Biqāʿī invokes prophets and community; Bint al-Shāṭiʾ cites 3:104, 9:71, 5:78–79. Quṭb stresses solidarity against ego and tyranny.

question: What does patience encompass?

positions.position: Persevering in obedience and required duties.
positions.reasons: Al-Ḥasan and Qatāda say obedience; Hishām b. Ḥassān says prescribed duties; Wahīdī includes striving.

positions.position: Obedience, restraint from sin, and endurance of trials, decree and harm.
positions.reasons: Zamakhsharī gives all three; Ibn Kathīr adds harm from those corrected. Tustarī cites 16:126–127; Elmalılı cites 3:200, 2:153 and 39:10; Bint al-Shāṭiʾ says the unstated object broadens scope.

positions.position: Self-restraint and moral training against desire and hardship.
positions.reasons: Jishumī defines restraint; Ibn ʿĀshūr excludes effort spent in sinful pleasure. Tustarī contrasts praiseworthy afterlife patience with worldly striving; Farāhī cites Ḥātim's verse.

positions.position: Inward and outward contentment with God's acts, in ease and trial.
positions.reasons: Qushayrī calls patience in well-being fullest and patience with God difficult; al-Ālūsī gives the rank of servitude; Sūlamī quotes a poem about concealed affliction.

positions.position: Courageous perseverance in good, never passive acceptance of wrong.
positions.reasons: Elmalılı cites the hadith of changing wrong by hand, speech or heart; 6:68 and 4:140 demand leaving mockery, and 12:108 insightful action.

turns_on: Whether it points to duties, comprehensive endurance, inward acceptance or active resolve.

question: Why repeat patience after truth?

positions.position: Patience is part of truth but singled out because defending truth is hard.
positions.reasons: Rāzī cites 31:17; Biqāʿī notes hostility; Ṭabāṭabāʾī points to the repeated verb; Quṭb stresses opposition and slow progress.

positions.position: The clauses mark complementary domains: truth to know or practice, patience to sustain it.
positions.reasons: Rāzī gives calling versus steadfastness; al-Ālūsī worship versus servitude; Farāhī truth as goal and patience as drive.

turns_on: Whether the second clause emphasizes an included virtue or distinguishes work.

question: What reading of biṣ-ṣabr is reported?

positions.position: Bāʾ can take slight kasra or ishām, generally explained as pause or transferred vowel.
positions.reasons: Abū ʿAmr, Salām, Hārūn and Ibn Mūsā are named. Ibn ʿAṭiyya and Aḥmad b. Mūsā restrict to pause; Abū ʿAlī allows rare connected speech as pause. ʿĪsā al-Baṣrī explains two sukūns; poetry illustrates transfer. Related reports mark al-ʿaṣr.

question: What expanded readings occur near the exception?

positions.position: The loss clause extends 'until the end of time'; one report adds 'calamities of time'.
positions.reasons: ʿAlī is linked to both; Saʿīd b. Jubayr, Ibrāhīm and Maymūn b. Mihrān connect the extension to Ibn Masʿūd.

question: Why state profit's cause but leave loss's cause vague?

positions.position: Loss may arise through sin or omitted obedience, while profit needs action; the focus suits divine generosity.
positions.reasons: Rāzī gives both explanations; Bayḍāwī says other pursuits lose or have reduced shares; Bursawī stresses eternal success.

question: What gain does the exception describe?

positions.position: Believers exchange transient life for lasting reward.
positions.reasons: Ibn Qutayba says reward is not diminished; Zamakhsharī and later sources use trade language. Rāzī consoles believers for lost youth. Elmalılı calls life loaned capital, citing 53:39 and 52:21.

positions.position: Old or sick believers keep credit for deeds from youth and health.
positions.reasons: Ibrāhīm's report parallels 95:4–6.

positions.position: Inwardly, escape yields perfected light and nearness beyond Paradise.
positions.reasons: Qāshānī describes passage beyond time; Biqāʿī distinguishes outward Paradise and inner light.

turns_on: Whether afterlife profit, continued credit or inward perfection is stressed.

question: What reports concern recitation and interpretation?

positions.position: Recitation brings forgiveness and placement among counselors of truth and patience.
positions.reasons: Zamakhsharī and Bayḍāwī transmit a Prophetic report, without grading in Bayḍāwī.

positions.position: Recitation brings patience and companionship with the truthful at Resurrection.
positions.reasons: Jishumī reports this from Ubayy.

positions.position: Two Companions recited the sura before parting and exchanged greetings.
positions.reasons: Abū Mulayka or Abū Madīna transmits this; Quṭb reads it as a renewed pledge.

positions.position: Al-Shāfiʿī said reflection on this sura suffices people.
positions.reasons: Bursawī also reports that it encompasses Qurʾānic learning.

positions.position: Ubayy asked the Prophet for its interpretation.
positions.reasons: Thaʿlabī introduces the report before the four Companion identifications.

positions.position: ʿAmr b. al-ʿĀṣ recited it to Musaylima, who answered with a failed parody.
positions.reasons: Ibn Kathīr places this before ʿAmr's conversion, describes the animal al-wabr and notes al-Kharāʾiṭī's version.

positions.position: Uways apologized for the hungry and unclothed and kept enjoining right despite insult.
positions.reasons: Tustarī reports his words on his only food and garment, death, God's claim on wealth and praise in every state.

turns_on: The reports describe different acts and promises.

question: How does the exception connect to other passages?

positions.position: It completes the warning of loss with the qualities that reverse it.
positions.reasons: Ibn ʿĀshūr sees the relative clause as explanatory; Study Quran compares 95:5–6 and Sura 102's rivalry.

positions.position: It parallels al-Balad's pairing of faith and counsel in patience and compassion.
positions.reasons: Bint al-Shāṭiʾ cites 90:11–17; Ṭabarī's patience citation is 90:17.

positions.position: After Sura 102, it distinguishes believers from people distracted by rivalry.
positions.reasons: Jishumī and Abū Ḥayyān give this link; Elmalılı relates counsel to 104:1.

positions.position: Another exception after descent to Hell parallels this escape from loss.
positions.reasons: Ṭabarī transmits this from Mujāhid and al-Ḥasan.

turns_on: Which neighbouring or parallel passage is used.

question: What overall life does the verse commend?

positions.position: Faith and personal good joined to communal care for truth, justice and endurance.
positions.reasons: Iṣlāḥī stresses individual and collective duties; Bint al-Shāṭiʾ social responsibility; Kur'an Yolu God's and others' rights. Quṭb invokes al-Nadwī's model of revealed, accountable, egalitarian leadership. Quṭb laments nationalist replacement of Islam's banner. Al-Nadwī praises early Muslim leadership: revealed law (6:122, 5:8), moral training, office as a trust (28:83, 4:58, 6:165), liberation from human servitude, equal dignity (49:13), ʿUmar's redress for an Egyptian, shared learning across peoples, and balanced spiritual and material civilization. Rabīʿ b. ʿĀmir's address to Yazdegerd illustrates its mission; Quṭb regards the Rightly Guided Caliphate as embodying the verse.

positions.position: The four qualities form a complete path to salvation and summarize Qurʾānic guidance.
positions.reasons: Quṭb says every other path loses; al-Shāfiʿī's reported saying supports sufficiency; Elmalılı sees life as capital.

positions.position: The verse also calls for inward transformation and valuing the present.
positions.reasons: Elmalılı reports the Sufi 'child of the moment'; Qāshānī sees affliction as divine discipline.

question: What historical allusions are drawn from its counts?

positions.position: Fourteen words indicate year fourteen of the mission and permission for jihad.
positions.reasons: Biqāʿī identifies Hijra and eventual triumph at Badr.

positions.position: Four basmala words added yield eighteen and evoke year five AH's campaigns.
positions.reasons: Biqāʿī cites 3:173 on enemy warnings and 33:10 on Confederate terror and the Prophet's subsequent declaration.

positions.position: Four pronouns point to year nine AH and Tabūk's hardship.
positions.reasons: Biqāʿī links patience to ensuing delegations and honor.

turns_on: Which count and event is correlated.

question: What is said about setting and verse division?

positions.position: The sura is generally Meccan, though Madinan attribution exists.
positions.reasons: Abū Ḥayyān names Ibn ʿAbbās, Ibn al-Zubayr and most authorities for Meccan; Mujāhid, Qatāda and Muqātil for Madinan. Ṭabāṭabāʾī favors Meccan; Asad and Study Quran place it after Sura 94.

positions.position: A divider after al-ḥaqq yields rhyme but separates parallel clauses.
positions.reasons: Medina II proposes it; Neuwirth objects.

positions.position: Verse 3 may be a later addition, explaining its unusual length.
positions.reasons: Corpus Coranicum notes phraseology characteristic of late Meccan and Medinan texts.

turns_on: The evidence concerns chronology and textual division.

question: How is loss outside the exception understood?

positions.position: Finite life expires without afterlife profit, culminating in reckoning.
positions.reasons: Ibn Qutayba glosses deficiency; Elmalılı likens life to loaned capital; Quṭb stresses Paradise and divine pleasure (78:40); Ṭabāṭabāʾī cites 13:26, 21:35, 53:39–41.

positions.position: The explicit exception means qualified believers are never in loss, limiting universal trade claims.
positions.reasons: Bint al-Shāṭiʾ rejects Zamakhsharī's trade metaphor and Rāzī's claim that permissible acts or imperfect worship always lose. She traces commercial and religious khusr (83:3, 55:9, 26:181) and rejects al-Rāghib's exclusively religious gloss.

turns_on: How literally to apply the commercial metaphor and the force of exemption.
